private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action; enforcement exclusively by FTC. Competitors may file complaints with FTC.

synthetic_media.detail: AI-generated fake reviews are explicitly prohibited as a form of synthetic deceptive content; rule is the first binding federal prohibition on AI-generated synthetic consumer deception.

biometric_data.detail: Rule does not address biometric data.

training_data_transparency.detail: Rule does not address AI training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Requires clear and conspicuous disclosure of material connections (compensation, employment) in reviews and testimonials; does not require AI-generated content labeling per se, but AI-generated fake reviews are prohibited outright.

anti_discrimination.detail: Rule does not address algorithmic discrimination or protected-class bias.

risk_classification.detail: Rule does not use a risk classification system; it is a specific conduct prohibition.

enforcement_model.detail: FTC civil penalty enforcement at up to $51,744 per violation; each day of violation is a separate violation. No criminal penalties under the rule itself.

operative_dates: Published August 14, 2024. Effective October 21, 2024.

full_name: Executive Order on Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence
preemption_notes: EO explicitly seeks to establish federal preemption of conflicting state AI laws; directs FTC to issue preemption statement and DOJ to litigate against conflicting state laws. Legal effectiveness of preemption subject to judicial review.
summary: Executive Order 14365, signed December 2025, directs the FTC to assert federal preemption of conflicting state AI laws, creates a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to challenge such laws in court, directs the FCC to consider a federal AI content disclosure standard, and conditions certain federal funding on states not enacting laws that conflict with national AI development priorities. The order reflects the Trump administration's strategy of using federal authority to prevent a patchwork of state AI regulations from impeding AI development.
notable: Trump administration's primary vehicle for federal preemption of state AI regulations. Creates DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to actively challenge state AI laws. Narrow carve-outs for children's safety laws and state AI procurement.
legal_citation: Exec. Order No. 14,365 (Dec. 11, 2025)
topics: federal preemption of state AI law
key_obligations: FTC directed to issue preemption policy statement on conflicting state AI laws within 120 days
DOJ directed to create AI Litigation Task Force to challenge conflicting state AI laws
FCC directed to initiate rulemaking on federal AI content disclosure standard within 90 days
OMB directed to issue updated federal AI governance framework within 180 days
Federal funding in certain categories conditioned on states not enacting conflicting AI laws

impact_assessment.detail: EO does not require impact assessments; it is a federal coordination and preemption directive.

prohibited_categories.detail: EO does not prohibit specific AI applications; it seeks to limit state-level AI prohibitions.

human_review_rights.detail: EO does not address individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Executive order; no private enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: EO does not address synthetic media specifically, though FCC rulemaking may eventually address AI content disclosure in broadcasting.

biometric_data.detail: EO does not address biometric data protection.

training_data_transparency.detail: EO does not address training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Directs FCC to initiate rulemaking on a federal AI content disclosure standard — intended to supersede conflicting state-level AI content labeling laws.

anti_discrimination.detail: EO does not address algorithmic discrimination or anti-discrimination standards.

risk_classification.detail: EO does not establish a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Primary enforcement mechanism is DOJ litigation against conflicting state AI laws, supplemented by federal funding conditions. No private enforcement or civil penalties.

operative_dates: Signed December 11, 2025. Agency deadlines: FCC rulemaking initiation within 90 days; FTC preemption statement within 120 days; OMB framework within 180 days.

full_name: Alabama House Bill 172 — Prohibition on Materially Deceptive AI-Generated Media in Elections
max_penalty: First offense: Class A misdemeanor (up to 1 year jail, $6,000 fine); subsequent offense within 5 years: Class C felony (1–10 years prison)
preemption_notes: No express preemption clause; operates alongside federal election and campaign finance laws
summary: Alabama HB 172 makes it a criminal offense to knowingly distribute materially deceptive AI-generated media intended to influence an election within 90 days before that election, and requires a prominent disclaimer for any AI-generated content used in political advertising. First violations are Class A misdemeanors; repeat violations within five years are Class C felonies. Satire and parody are exempted.
legal_citation: Alabama HB 172 (2024 Regular Session); Ala. Code § [TBD]
key_obligations: Criminal prohibition on distributing materially deceptive AI-generated media within 90 days of an election with intent to influence
Required prominent disclaimer for AI-generated content in political advertising
First violation: Class A misdemeanor; subsequent violation within 5 years: Class C felony

impact_assessment.detail: Law does not require impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits distribution of materially deceptive AI-generated media in election campaigns within 90 days of an election with intent to influence.

human_review_rights.detail: Law does not address individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Criminal prosecution only by Attorney General or District Attorneys; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Prohibits materially deceptive AI-generated media in elections; requires disclosure for non-deceptive AI-generated political content.

biometric_data.detail: Law does not specifically address biometric data.

training_data_transparency.detail: Law does not address training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Requires prominent disclosure that political advertising content is AI-generated.

anti_discrimination.detail: Law does not address algorithmic discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: Law does not use a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal enforcement by AG and District Attorneys. Class A misdemeanor for first offense; Class C felony for repeat offense within 5 years.

operative_dates: Enacted April 24, 2024. Effective October 1, 2024.

full_name: Alabama House Bill 161 — Prohibition on Nonconsensual AI-Generated Intimate Images
max_penalty: Class A misdemeanor (criminal); civil liability to victim including actual damages, statutory damages, and punitive damages
preemption_notes: No express preemption clause; operates alongside federal law including potential Section 230 questions for platforms
summary: Alabama HB 161 prohibits the creation and distribution of nonconsensual AI-generated sexually explicit images of identifiable real persons, including both fully AI-generated images and AI-manipulated real photographs, providing criminal penalties (Class A misdemeanor) and a private civil cause of action for victims including actual, statutory, and punitive damages.
legal_citation: Alabama HB 161 (2024 Regular Session); Ala. Code § [TBD]
key_obligations: Prohibition on creating AI-generated sexually explicit images of identifiable persons without consent
Prohibition on distributing such images without consent
Criminal penalty: Class A misdemeanor for first offense
Civil cause of action for victims including actual damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees

impact_assessment.detail: Law does not require impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits creation and distribution of nonconsensual AI-generated sexually explicit depictions of identifiable persons.

human_review_rights.detail: Law does not address rights to human review of AI decisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Victims have an explicit private civil cause of action for actual damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees against creators and distributors of nonconsensual AI-generated intimate images.

synthetic_media.detail: Prohibits AI-generated and AI-manipulated sexually explicit depictions of identifiable persons absent explicit consent. Covers both fully synthetic images and real-image manipulation.

biometric_data.detail: Law does not address biometric data protection directly; identity protection in intimate context addressed through NCII prohibition.

training_data_transparency.detail: Law does not address training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Law does not require content labeling; it prohibits the covered content outright.

anti_discrimination.detail: Law does not address algorithmic discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: Law does not use a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal enforcement by AG and District Attorneys (Class A misdemeanor); private civil action by victims. Both tracks available independently.

operative_dates: Enacted April 24, 2024. Effective October 1, 2024.

full_name: Delaware House Bill 333 — Delaware Artificial Intelligence Commission Act
preemption_notes: Study and advisory body only; no preemption implications
summary: Delaware HB 333 establishes the Delaware Artificial Intelligence Commission within the Office of the State Auditor, charged with assessing AI risks and benefits across all three branches of state government, recommending AI governance and procurement standards, and reporting annually to the legislature. The Commission has no enforcement powers and imposes no obligations on private industry, and is scheduled to automatically terminate after 10 years.
legal_citation: Delaware HB 333, 153rd General Assembly (2024)
key_obligations: Establishes Delaware AI Commission within Office of State Auditor
Commission to assess AI risks and benefits across all three branches of state government
Commission to recommend AI governance and procurement standards
Annual reporting to Governor and General Assembly
Commission auto-terminates after 10 years

impact_assessment.detail: Commission will study and may recommend impact assessment requirements, but the Act itself does not require impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: Act does not prohibit any AI applications; may recommend prohibitions through future legislative recommendations.

human_review_rights.detail: Act does not address individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Act creates no private rights or enforcement mechanisms.

synthetic_media.detail: Act does not address synthetic media specifically; within scope of Commission's broad study mandate.

biometric_data.detail: Act does not address biometric data; within scope of Commission's study mandate.

training_data_transparency.detail: Act does not address training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Act does not address content labeling.

anti_discrimination.detail: Act does not address algorithmic discrimination; within scope of Commission's study mandate.

risk_classification.detail: Act does not establish a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Commission is advisory only; no enforcement powers or penalty structure.

operative_dates: Enacted and effective July 17, 2024. Commission auto-terminates July 17, 2034.

full_name: Hawaii Senate Bill 2687 / Act 191 — Prohibition on Materially Deceptive AI-Generated Deepfakes in Elections
max_penalty: Civil penalties; criminal misdemeanor (enforcement permanently enjoined as of early 2026)
preemption_notes: No express preemption clause; law is unenforceable due to permanent federal court injunction on First Amendment grounds
summary: Hawaii Act 191 (SB 2687) prohibited materially deceptive AI-generated media in election campaigns without a prominent disclaimer and provided for civil and criminal enforcement, but enforcement was permanently enjoined by a federal court in early 2026 on First Amendment grounds. The law remains on the books but is unenforceable, making it a significant reference case in national debates about the constitutionality of AI deepfake election laws.
notable: Federal court permanently enjoined enforcement on First Amendment grounds. Law remains on books but unenforceable. Key reference case for constitutionality of state AI deepfake election laws.
legal_citation: Hawaii Act 191 of 2024 (SB 2687)
topics: First Amendment challenges to AI law
key_obligations: Prohibition on distributing materially deceptive AI-generated media in election campaigns within 90 days of election (enjoined)
Required prominent disclaimer for AI-generated political media (enjoined)
Civil and criminal enforcement by Hawaii AG (enjoined)

impact_assessment.detail: Law does not require impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibited materially deceptive AI-generated media in elections; enforcement permanently enjoined on First Amendment grounds.

human_review_rights.detail: Law does not address rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: AG enforcement only; no private right of action. Enforcement permanently enjoined.

synthetic_media.detail: Prohibited materially deceptive AI-generated deepfakes in elections; required disclaimer for AI-generated political content. Permanently enjoined from enforcement.

biometric_data.detail: Law does not address biometric data.

training_data_transparency.detail: Law does not address training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Required prominent disclaimer for AI-generated election media. Enjoined from enforcement.

anti_discrimination.detail: Law does not address algorithmic discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: Law does not use a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Civil penalties and criminal misdemeanor by AG. Permanently enjoined from enforcement on First Amendment grounds as of early 2026.

operative_dates: Enacted July 3, 2024. Effective July 3, 2024. Enforcement permanently enjoined by federal court, early 2026.

full_name: Mississippi Senate Bill 2426 — Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Regulation Task Force Act
preemption_notes: Study and advisory body only; no preemption implications
summary: Mississippi SB 2426 establishes the Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Regulation (AIR) Task Force, a multi-stakeholder body including legislators, executive officials, and industry representatives, charged with studying AI risks and benefits, reviewing national regulatory developments, and recommending legislation to the Mississippi Legislature through annual reports by December 2027. The Task Force has no enforcement powers and imposes no obligations on private AI developers or deployers.
legal_citation: Mississippi SB 2426 (2025 Regular Session)
key_obligations: Establishes Mississippi AIR Task Force with legislators, executive officials, and industry representatives

full_name: European Commission Guidelines on the Scope of Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models (Article 53 EU AI Act)
preemption_notes: Commission Guidelines under Article 96 EU AI Act; bind national competent authorities in enforcement interpretation; GPAI Code of Practice compliance creates rebuttable presumption of conformity
summary: Binding interpretive guidelines published by the European Commission on 18 July 2025 under Article 96 of the EU AI Act, clarifying which AI models qualify as General-Purpose AI Models and the specific compliance obligations for GPAI model providers under Article 53. Establishes the 10²³ FLOPs compute threshold for GPAI model classification and the 10²⁵ FLOPs threshold for systemic risk designation. Covers technical documentation, training data summaries, copyright compliance policies, and incident reporting requirements. Legally distinct from the non-binding GPAI Code of Practice.
notable: Hard-law interpretive instrument — distinct from the voluntary GPAI Code of Practice. Compliance with the Code creates a rebuttable presumption of conformity with these Guidelines.
legal_citation: EU AI Act Art. 53, Art. 55, Art. 96; Annex XI, XIII
key_obligations: Maintain and publish technical documentation (Annex XI)
Publish sufficiently detailed training data summary
Implement and publish copyright compliance policy with opt-out mechanism
Provide technical documentation to downstream providers
Report serious incidents to EU AI Office
Systemic-risk models: adversarial testing, cybersecurity measures, 24-hour incident reporting

impact_assessment.detail: Systemic-risk GPAI models (≥10²⁵ FLOPs) must conduct model evaluation including adversarial testing; all GPAI providers must assess risks documented in technical documentation.

prohibited_categories.detail: Guidelines focus on GPAI model obligations; prohibited AI practices are addressed in EU AI Act Article 5 and separate instruments.

human_review_rights.detail: GPAI Guidelines do not create individual human review rights; those are addressed under deployer-level AI Act obligations.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement is by EU AI Office and national competent authorities; no private right of action created.

synthetic_media.detail: Content labelling for synthetic media is addressed in EU AI Act transparency obligations; these Guidelines focus on GPAI model provider obligations upstream.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed in GPAI Guidelines.

training_data_transparency.detail: Providers must publish training data summary covering major data categories, geographical and temporal coverage, and language composition; detailed documentation provided to EU AI Office on request.

content_labeling.detail: Content labelling is a downstream deployer obligation; GPAI Guidelines address upstream model provider obligations.

anti_discrimination.detail: Not directly addressed in GPAI Guidelines.

risk_classification.detail: 10²³ FLOPs threshold for GPAI model classification; 10²⁵ FLOPs for systemic risk designation; systemic risk also determinable by Commission on other criteria including user reach and capability evaluations.

enforcement_model.detail: EU AI Office as primary enforcer for GPAI obligations; national competent authorities for downstream; penalties up to 3% global turnover for Article 53/55 violations.

private_right_of_action.detail: No changes to enforcement model proposed.

risk_classification.detail: Risk classification tiers unchanged; proposal only adjusts compliance timelines.
